world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Edel (1939) The Tillamook Language, IJAL 10; Thompson & Thompson (1966) A Fresh Look at Tillamook Phonology, IJAL 32 - both JSTOR-paywalled

new_statements.quote: The salient phonological processes impacting morphological analysis ultimately involve stress assignment in the underlying form. Valences for stress (i.e., weak versus strong) and interaction of roots and suffixes concerning stress retention or loss, if any, have yet to be worked out. There is a very strong tendency toward penultimate stress, however, with attendant vowel reduction and consonantal adjustments. [...] One other phonological rule is necessary to allow the pieces of the morphological puzzle to fit together and still follow the rule fixing penultimate stress. Certain vowel adjustments, such as //V-ə// > V, occur before stress is fixed on the penultimate vowel.
new_statements.citation: Egesdal, Steven M. & M. Terry Thompson. 1996. A Fresh Look at Tillamook Inflectional Morphology. Papers for the 31st International Conference on Salish and Neighbouring Languages (ICSNL 31). Honolulu: University of Hawaii.
new_statements.locator: §3.1 Synchronic changes, pp. 2-3 of the paper (running-foot page numbers; first page carries proceedings no. 143). Exceptions: p. 8 (independent pronominals), p. 10 (conjunctive enclitics), fn. 33.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the underlying (pre-reduction) form of the predicative word, i.e. counting the full underlying vowels of root + suffixes (+ enclitic conjunctive pronominals) before unstressed vowels reduce or delete; surface forms therefore often look irregular. The authors call it a 'very strong tendency' rather than an exceptionless law and say root/suffix stress valences are not yet worked out.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. (Edel 1939: 12 had noted that 'more than one syllable in a word may be stressed' and that a raised pitch is integral with stress, but admitted stress was inadequately recorded.)
new_statements.exceptions: Independent (emphatic) pronominals 'retain the original stress of PS, which explains why the forms do not show expected penultimate stress' (p. 8); certain vowel coalescences apply before stress assignment, e.g. the 2sObj-1sSbj sequence where final stress would otherwise be expected (fn. 33); unstressed schwa/vowel reduction and consonant adjustments follow stress assignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the full predicative word in its underlying form, including enclitic conjunctive pronominals ('they become part of the preceding predicative for stress assignment', p. 10); particles (e.g. article də) do not take primary stress. Based on the Thompsons' 1960s field notes with the last speakers, checked against Jacobs's 1930s notes and Edel 1939.
new_statements.identity_note: Tillamook proper (Glottolog till1254, ISO til; self-name Hutyéyu), an extinct Oregon Coast Salish language. The quoted statement rests on the Thompsons' 1960s field notes with the last speakers (northern/Tillamook Bay-Nehalem variety), cross-checked with Jacobs's 1930s notes and Edel's 1939 sketch, which is explicitly 'based upon material from the northern dialect' (Edel 1939: 2); the southern Siletz dialect is known only from Boas 1890 and Frachtenberg 1910 wordlists and is not described for stress.

sources.citation: Edel, May M. 1939. The Tillamook Language. International Journal of American Linguistics 10(1): 1-57 (= Columbia dissertation 1940). §14 Stress, p. 12 (PDF p. 16).
sources.note: §14 Stress, p. 12: 'More than one syllable in a word may be stressed. Jacobs calls attention to the fact that there is a raised pitch, "anywhere from a second to a fifth", which is integral with stress. Unfortunately, stress was not very adequately recorded. The following tentative suggestions are mostly Jacobs'. The presence of a suffix in many cases affects the stress. -s gives the accent to the final syllable... -i lengthens the vowel of the preceding syllable, which then carries the stress, sometimes taking it away from the penult which in other forms may have the accent.' Also p. 25: vow…
Phonology section covers consonants/vowels only; nothing on stress. Its reference list pointed to the open UBC ICSNL PDF (Egesdal & Thompson 1996).
